newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - Chiang Kai-shek still reviled in China.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Chiang Kai-shek still reviled in China.

text.p: Rusty handcuffs, manacles and nail-studded clubs litter a dimly-lit torture chamber at the Zhazidong prison in China's wartime capital of Chongqing.

A faded photograph of the late Nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek, who fled into exile in Taiwan with his defeated armies in 1949, hangs on a wall of the old torture chamber -- now a museum that serves as a grim reminder of his "crimes".
"Chiang Kai-shek's hands are stained with the blood of Communist Party members and the masses," the Chongqing Evening News screamed in an edition last year.

Nationalist soldiers executed scores of political prisoners, mostly Communist Party members, and set fire to Zhazidong prison before fleeing Chongqing, which was about to be overrun by the Red Army as the Chinese civil war drew to an end.
Chiang, who died in Taiwan in 1975, is still officially one of the most reviled men in communist China.
Beijing ignores Chiang's role as leader of the resistance against Japanese invaders in the 1930s and 1940s. Most schoolchildren are told that ill-equipped communist guerrillas did all the fighting.
ADVERTISING GIMMICK BACKFIRES
A mineral water bottler in Chongqing was forced to stop production last August after coming under fire from the state media for trying to cash in on Chiang's name.
The Chongqing Evening News accused the bottler of "using Chiang's soul to solicit business".

The bottler had said in advertisements its mineral water came from a well that Chiang alone drank from during his stay in Chongqing. Chiang had made the foggy, mountain city China's wartime capital from 1938 to 1945.
"Not only were there no new orders, stores returned our goods," said a worker at the bottling company.
Chiang is without exception portrayed as the bad guy in Chinese movies and China's history books describe him as the "common enemy of the people".
Understandably, many people have no kind words for Chiang.
"Chiang Kai-shek killed many people... He once said: 'Better to kill a thousand in error than to let one (communist) go'," said a Beijing resident.
Chiang's nemesis, Mao Zedong, once called him "China's number one war criminal".
The Nationalist leader was instrumental in the jailing and execution of thousands during a purge of Communist Party members in Shanghai and Nanjing in 1927.
KIDNAPPER HAILED AS HERO IN CHINA
A few hundred metres from Zhazidong prison is what China says is further testimony to Chiang's ruthlessness -- the former villa of the notorious Nationalist intelligence chief Tai Li.
General Yang Hu-cheng, former commander of China's northwest army, his son, an aide and the aide's family were assassinated by Chiang's henchmen at the villa in September 1949.

Yang and the former commander of China's northeast army had kidnapped Chiang in the ancient Chinese capital of Xian in December 1936 to force Chiang to end his feud with the communists and join forces to fight invading Japanese troops.
The abduction changed Chinese history, giving a new lease on life to the Red Army, which was on the verge of being wiped out by the Nationalists.
Yang is hailed as a hero in China. The villa where he was assassinated has been turned into a museum and is a popular tourist attraction.
Chiang's embalmed remains are also popular with tourists, though generally not those from China. His casket rests in Taiwan as he never realised his dream of recapturing the Chinese mainland.
Last year, Taiwan blocked a bid by Chiang's surviving family members to bury him in China.
If Taipei and Beijing ever agree to allow a return of Chiang's remains, the reception on the mainland might not be all negative.
"I'm a Communist Party member, so I think Chiang Kai-shek is a criminal," said Xiong Zhouqing, a 23-year-old Chongqing resident.
"But if I were not a communist, maybe my view would be different," she said.
